content: The risk of bacterial vaginosis, certain sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), and HIV is significant. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV and antiretroviral therapy (ART) for STDs have the potential to influence both the transmission and acquisition of HIV. In individuals infected with HIV, ART reduces the viral load and likely decreases their infectiousness. For individuals not infected with HIV, ART may reduce their susceptibility to infection. This concept is supported by both animal studies and a study on safety and acceptability conducted among West African women. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving South African women demonstrated that the use of tenofovir gel during sexual intercourse significantly reduced the acquisition rates of HIV and herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) by 39% and 51%, respectively. Several large randomized controlled trials of PrEP are currently underway or planned. These trials involve the oral use of non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, such as tenofovir or tenofovir-emtricitabine, or the vaginal use of 1% tenofovir gel. Retesting for chlamydia or gonorrhea several months after an initial diagnosis can help detect repeat infections and may enhance population-based prevention efforts. Further details on retesting are available in the specific sections on chlamydia and gonorrhea within this report. Partner management refers to a range of activities aimed at increasing the number of infected individuals who receive treatment and disrupting transmission networks. A key component of this process is partner notification, where healthcare providers or public health authorities identify the sexual or needle-sharing partners of infected patients and facilitate their evaluation and treatment. Clinical-care providers can directly obtain this information and arrange for partner evaluation and treatment or collaborate with state and local health departments to do so. The scope and comprehensiveness of partner services, as well as the specific STDs for which they are offered, vary by provider, public health agency, and geographic location. Ideally, individuals referred to such services should also receive health counseling and be directed to other appropriate health services. Data on the effectiveness of partner notification in reducing exposure to STDs and decreasing the incidence and prevalence of these infections in a community are limited. However, evaluations of partner notification interventions have documented the significant role this approach can play in identifying cases in both clinical and community settings. When partners are treated, the risk of reinfection for the index patient is reduced. Therefore, providers should encourage individuals with STDs to notify their sexual partners and urge them to seek medical evaluation and treatment. Providers can also ask patients to bring their partners with them when returning for treatment. Counseling index patients on the importance of notifying partners has been associated with improved notification outcomes. When patients diagnosed with chlamydia or gonorrhea indicate that their partners are unlikely to seek evaluation and treatment, providers can offer patient-delivered partner therapy (PDPT). This is a form of expedited partner therapy (EPT) in which the partners of infected individuals are treated without prior medical evaluation or prevention counseling. Providers should consult updated information for their specific jurisdiction regarding EPT. Any medication or prescription provided for PDPT should include treatment instructions, appropriate warnings (e.g., for pregnant partners or those with medication allergies), general health counseling, and a statement advising partners to seek personal medical evaluation, particularly women with symptoms of STDs or pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). The evidence supporting PDPT is based on three clinical trials that included heterosexual men and women diagnosed with chlamydia or gonorrhea.
